We validate the static position-dependent-mass (PDM) eigensolver through two stringent benchmarks: a comparison to the analytical Quesne PDM model and a [MATH] double quantum well, where the exponential decay of computed tunnel splittings follows Wentzel-Kramers-Brillouin (WKB) theory at the sub-percent level. We further demonstrate the time-propagation engine on constant-mass systems, accurately reproducing high-harmonic generation (HHG) spectra in atomic benchmarks and confirming the importance of dimensionality in fully capturing the strong light-matter interaction. Our implementation demonstrates robust strong-scaling efficiency, maintaining performance across hundreds of CPU cores. While the static eigensolver currently supports optional GPU offloading, the time-propagation engine is CPU-optimised, providing a modular architecture for future expansion toward exascale quantum dynamics.
tldr: This paper introduces a high-performance open-source framework for simulating strong-field quantum dynamics in atomic, molecular, and semiconductor systems using a weak-form Galerkin discretisation of the BenDaniel-Duke operator on B-spline meshes.
motivation: To address the need for robust and efficient numerical simulations of strong-field quantum dynamics in heterogeneous systems, enabling studies of high-harmonic generation and related phenomena.
method: The implementation uses a weak-form Galerkin discretisation of the Hermitian BenDaniel-Duke operator on geometry-adapted B-spline meshes, supporting arbitrary potentials and laser configurations in 1-3 dimensions, with CPU and optional GPU acceleration.
result: Validation against analytical models and WKB theory shows sub-percent accuracy, and time-propagation reproduces high-harmonic generation spectra correctly, demonstrating strong scaling across hundreds of CPU cores.
conclusion: The framework provides a flexible, scalable tool for strong-field dynamics simulations across atomic, molecular, and semiconductor systems, with potential for exascale computing.

title: Propagation Of Laguerre-Gaussian And Bessel-Gaussian Scalar Beams In An Effective Anisotropic Background
authors: C. A. Escobar, Rom\'an Linares, E. Pl\'acido-Flores
abstract: ArXiv:2608.18478v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the propagation of structured scalar optical beams in an effective anisotropic background inspired by the scalar sector of the Standard-Model Extension and controlled by a single dimensionless parameter [MATH]. The physically relevant configuration is a transverse radial director field that modifies the radial part of the Helmholtz operator while preserving axial symmetry. Starting from the Green-function representation, we cast the propagation problem as an initial-value spectral reconstruction of a prescribed finite-aperture entrance profile at [MATH] and verify that this profile is recovered at the launch plane across the values of [MATH] used in the analysis, within small numerical error. We use the Laguerre--Gaussian mode [MATH] as the representative vortex-free Laguerre case, retain [MATH] only as a quantitative benchmark for radial-order dependence, and compare both with a Bessel--Gaussian beam of input order [MATH]. The effective anisotropy produces a systematic redistribution of radial intensity, determines whether the central peak remains dominant or is overtaken by off-axis maxima as propagation advances, and controls the radial displacement of the dominant side lobes. For the finite-aperture Bessel--Gaussian beam, the same parameter quantifies how the approximately diffraction-resistant ring structure broadens for negative [MATH] and compresses for positive [MATH] during propagation.
tldr: Investigates propagation of structured scalar optical beams in an anisotropic background inspired by the Standard-Model Extension.
motivation: To understand how an effective anisotropic background affects the propagation of structured light beams.
method: Uses Green-function representation and spectral reconstruction to analyze propagation of Laguerre-Gaussian and Bessel-Gaussian beams.
result: Anisotropy causes radial intensity redistribution and changes in beam structure during propagation.
conclusion: The anisotropy parameter controls beam evolution and can broaden or compress ring structures.

title: Sampling Isometric Tensor Network States With Monitored Quantum Circuits
authors: Yuqing Rong, Huan-Hai Zhou, Guo-Yi Zhu, Jinguo Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2608.18511v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Projected entangled pair states (PEPS) provide an efficient variational ansatz for two-dimensional quantum phases, but computing observables remains challenging because PEPS contraction is generally costly. Here, we parameterize two-dimensional quantum states using variational PEPS subject to isometric constraints and map the resulting ansatz onto monitored quantum circuits, replacing tensor-network contraction with circuit sampling. For infinite cylinders, the transfer matrix defines a quantum channel on the virtual boundary. We use a fixed-point treatment and a monitored-circuit unraveling of this channel to evaluate observables efficiently. Using a constant number of variational parameters and a number of qubits that scales only with the cylinder width, our method yields a phase diagram for the [MATH]-[MATH] model in qualitative agreement with DMRG results. Because the monitored circuits are compatible with near-term quantum hardware, this approach provides a hybrid quantum-classical framework for simulating two-dimensional quantum many-body systems.
tldr: This paper proposes a hybrid quantum-classical method to simulate 2D quantum many-body systems by mapping isometric PEPS to monitored quantum circuits, avoiding costly tensor network contraction.
motivation: Computing observables from PEPS is computationally expensive due to contraction complexity. The authors aim to leverage quantum hardware to sample from the state instead of contracting.
method: They parameterize 2D quantum states with isometric PEPS, map the ansatz to monitored quantum circuits, and use a fixed-point treatment and monitored-circuit unraveling of the transfer matrix for infinite cylinders to compute observables via circuit sampling.
result: They produce a phase diagram for the J1-J2 model in qualitative agreement with DMRG, using a constant number of variational parameters and a number of qubits scaling only with the cylinder width.
conclusion: This approach offers a feasible route for simulating 2D quantum systems on near-term quantum hardware.

title: Know Your Qubits, Know Your Users: Personas For Quantum Software
authors: Lukas Schmidbauer, Joshua Ammermann, Laura Schulz, Jose Garcia-Alonso, Robert Wille, Sebastian Feld, Ina Schaefer, Wolfgang Mauerer
abstract: ArXiv:2608.18598v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The advancement of quantum hardware and the intricacies of quantum computing make well-designed quantum software increasingly necessary. Due to the interdisciplinarity of the field, it is crucial to understand the perspectives and specific needs of involved stakeholders, for example, to balance the desired level of abstraction with the exposition of (hardware)-specific details. In this work, we conduct a stakeholder-based analysis to identify personas of quantum software as a means of creating meaningful, user-tailored quantum software. We conducted an expert focus group at a Dagstuhl seminar in 2024 and qualitative interviews with practitioners at conference IEEE QCE in 2025, from which we derive eleven personas of potential users and stakeholders for quantum software. We discuss these personas regarding their use cases, interests, constraints and abstraction level.
tldr: This paper defines eleven personas for quantum software users based on stakeholder analysis, aiming to guide user-tailored software design.
motivation: The interdisciplinary nature of quantum computing requires understanding the diverse needs and abstraction preferences of stakeholders to improve quantum software usability.
method: The authors conducted an expert focus group at a Dagstuhl seminar and qualitative interviews with practitioners at IEEE QCE, from which they derived eleven personas.
result: They present eleven personas for potential users and stakeholders of quantum software, discussing their use cases, interests, constraints, and abstraction levels.
conclusion: The study provides a foundation for designing quantum software that addresses the varied perspectives and requirements of its users.

title: Comparative Study Of Nonperturbative Electron-positron Pair Production By Intense Laser Fields Colliding With Either Bremsstrahlung $\gamma$-rays Or Relativistic Ions
authors: S. Remme, A. B. Voitkiv, S. Villalba-Ch\'avez, C. M\"uller
abstract: ArXiv:2608.18718v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: It is well known that electron-positron pairs can be created in the strong-field environments formed by (i) a high-intensity laser field and a high-energy [MATH]-photon (nonlinear Breit-Wheeler process) or (ii) a high-intensity laser field and a nuclear Coulomb field (nonlinear Bethe-Heitler process). Both of these processes are particularly interesting in the interaction regime where the laser field enters nonperturbatively. Various experimental collaborations are currently aiming at detecting for the first time the nonperturbative Breit-Wheeler process, by exploiting high-intensity laser pulses and [MATH]-ray sources based on bremsstrahlung. In contrast, an experimental observation of the nonlinear, nonperturbative Bethe-Heitler process still lies further ahead in the future because its technical realization appears at present more challenging. Our comparative study shows, however, that the physical properties of the total rates for the processes (i) and (ii) can become remarkably similar when the parameters for the bremsstrahlung-driven nonperturbative Breit-Wheeler process are properly chosen. In this sense, the upcoming experiments on the nonlinear Breit-Wheeler process could also be used to closely ``simulate'' the currently hard to observe nonlinear Bethe-Heitler process.
tldr: This paper compares nonperturbative electron-positron pair production via the nonlinear Breit-Wheeler and Bethe-Heitler processes and suggests that upcoming experiments on the former could simulate the latter.
motivation: Both processes are important in strong-field QED but the Bethe-Heitler process is harder to observe experimentally; the study aims to show similarity under proper parameter choices.
method: A comparative theoretical study of the total rates for both processes, analyzing how parameters can be chosen to make them similar.
result: The physical properties of the total rates become remarkably similar when parameters for the bremsstrahlung-driven Breit-Wheeler process are properly chosen.
conclusion: Experiments on the nonlinear Breit-Wheeler process could closely simulate the currently hard-to-observe nonlinear Bethe-Heitler process.

title: $Ab$ $initio$ Calculation Of Hyperfine-structure Properties To Extract Nuclear Magnetic Octupole Moments Of $^{69}$Ga And $^{71}$Ga
authors: Fei-Chen Li (school Of Physics And Advanced Energy, Henan University Of Technology, Zhengzhou, China), Yong-Bo Tang
abstract: ArXiv:2608.18811v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We calculate the hyperfine-structure properties of the low-lying states in [MATH]Ga and [MATH]Ga using the relativistic coupled-cluster method at the singles and doubles (RCCSD) level. The properties include the first-order hyperfine constants and the second-order corrections arising from off-diagonal hyperfine interactions. Based on our theoretical results, we reanalyze the previous hyperfine-splitting measurements of the [MATH] state in [MATH]Ga [R. T. Daly and J. H. Holloway, Phys. Rev. 96, 539 (1954)], and refine the nuclear magnetic octupole moments of these two isotopes. The refined values [MATH] and [MATH] are about 13\% and 12\% larger than the earlier results reported by Daly and Holloway. By providing the first independent determination, the present results offer a reliable set of reference values for the magnetic octupole moments of [MATH]Ga, which will benefit both future high-precision measurements and nuclear-structure calculations.
tldr: The paper uses relativistic coupled-cluster method to calculate hyperfine-structure properties and refine nuclear magnetic octupole moments of gallium isotopes.
motivation: To provide accurate nuclear magnetic octupole moments for gallium isotopes for nuclear structure studies and high-precision measurements.
method: Relativistic coupled-cluster singles and doubles (RCCSD) method to compute hyperfine constants and second-order corrections.
result: Refined values are about 13% and 12% larger than earlier results.
conclusion: The results provide reliable reference values for future measurements and nuclear-structure calculations.

title: Tobyqa: A Trust-Region Method For Derivative-Free Optimization On Time-Varying Functions
authors: Pengcheng Xie Haoyu Yao
abstract: ArXiv:2608.18124v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Derivative-free optimization (DFO) becomes particularly difficult when function evaluations are affected by temporal drift and observation noise. Conventional trust-region methods generally assume a static landscape, which may lead to stale-data bias and misleading trust-region updates. We propose TOBYQA (Time-augmented Optimization BY Quadratic Approximation), a regularized DFO framework that jointly models spatial geometry and temporal variations within a unified quadratic interpolation system. Specifically, TOBYQA augments the classical KKT interpolation system with a ridge term on the [MATH]-block, which accommodates observation noise and ensures well-posedness under a mild full-column-rank condition on the constraint block, thereby relaxing the stringent geometric poisedness requirements of classical methods. To handle non-stationarity, we embed an explicit linear-in-time drift term into the interpolation model, enabling a drift-compensated ratio test that subtracts the estimated temporal component from the observed reduction. Additionally, a diagonal affine-scaling adapts the search geometry to local variation in curvature. Benchmark evaluations on the Mor\'e--Wild 88-function suite across various temporal drifts and dimensions ([MATH]) demonstrate that TOBYQA exhibits enhanced robustness under drift, while maintaining competitive performance in static environments.
tldr: TOBYQA is a trust-region derivative-free optimization method that handles time-varying functions by augmenting the interpolation model with temporal terms.
motivation: Standard derivative-free optimization methods assume static landscapes, which can lead to stale data and poor performance when functions drift over time.
method: It adds a ridge term to the KKT system for noise robustness and an explicit linear-in-time drift term, plus diagonal affine scaling to adapt to local curvature.
result: Benchmarks on the Moré–Wild 88-function suite show enhanced robustness under temporal drift while maintaining competitive performance in static environments.
conclusion: TOBYQA improves derivative-free optimization on time-varying functions, offering a reliable approach when temporal drift and observation noise are present.

title: Combinatorial Car T-cell Circuit Design Using Single- And Multi-Objective Local Search
authors: Bartol Borozan, Alice Descoeudres, Aneta Neumann, Frank Neumann, Stefan Canzar
abstract: ArXiv:2608.18127v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: CAR T-cell circuit design enables targeting tumour cells while keeping healthy cells unaffected to a cancer treatment. Designing CAR T-cell circuits that maximize the number of tumour cells eliminated (called efficacy) while meeting the safety constraint of keeping a large number of healthy cells unaffected is a challenging task. We provide a new multistart local search approach for this problem and show that it outperforms the current SOTA approach on a single-cell cancer atlas. Furthermore, we introduce a multi-objective local search approach which provides insights into the trade-offs of efficacy and safety of the treatment. Our experiments also demonstrate that the multi-objective approach yields improved solutions even for the constrained single-objective optimisation problem.
tldr: This paper presents local search algorithms for optimizing CAR T-cell circuit design in cancer treatment, focusing on efficacy and safety trade-offs.
motivation: Designing CAR T-cell circuits that maximize tumor cell elimination while preserving healthy cells is challenging; current methods may not achieve optimal trade-offs.
method: The authors introduce a multistart local search approach and a multi-objective local search approach to explore efficacy-safety trade-offs.
result: Their methods outperform the state-of-the-art on a single-cell cancer atlas and provide insights into trade-offs.
conclusion: Multi-objective local search yields improved solutions for constrained single-objective problems and offers better understanding of trade-offs.

title: Nearest Graph Laplacians With Prescribed Connected Components: A Convex Framework For Network Reconstruction
authors: Udit Raj, Sudeepto Bhattacharya, Prince Kanhya
abstract: ArXiv:2608.18128v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the problem of constructing the nearest graph Laplacian matrix to a given Laplacian while enforcing a prescribed connected-component structure. Let the vertex set be partitioned into nonempty disjoint blocks [MATH], and let [MATH] be the matrix of the corresponding block-indicator vectors. The constraint [MATH] ensures that these prescribed indicators lie in the nullspace of the optimized Laplacian [MATH], and hence the associated graph has at least [MATH] connected components. To guarantee exactly the prescribed components, we impose additional block-connectivity constraints on the principal blocks [MATH]. These constraints ensure that each prescribed block induces a connected weighted subgraph. The resulting problem is a convex semidefinite optimization problem with a strictly convex Frobenius-norm objective. We prove existence and uniqueness of the minimizer and show that the optimized Laplacian has exactly the prescribed connected components, with nullspace [MATH]. The framework proposed in this work provides a principled tool for quantifying the minimum structural intervention required to transform a graph-based network into one having a prescribed group-separated structure. Numerical examples, including the Sampson monastery positive-affection network, illustrate the nearest faction-consistent weighted reconstruction and the minimum Laplacian perturbation required to realize the prescribed faction structure.
tldr: This paper proposes a convex optimization method to find the nearest graph Laplacian (in Frobenius norm) that imposes a prescribed connected-component structure on the graph.
motivation: The goal is to quantify the minimal structural modification needed to transform a given network into one with a specified group-separated topology, such as faction structures in social networks.
method: The problem is formulated as a convex semidefinite program with constraints ensuring the block-indicator vectors lie in the nullspace of the Laplacian and that each prescribed block induces a connected subgraph; existence and uniqueness of the minimizer are proven.
result: The optimized Laplacian is proven to have exactly the prescribed connected components, and numerical examples, including the Sampson monastery network, demonstrate the approach's effectiveness in network reconstruction.
conclusion: The framework provides a principled and computationally tractable tool for network reconstruction with predefined connectivity constraints, with applications in social network analysis and beyond.

title: Simulation-Optimization Of Systems Of Optimizers: Exploiting The Inner Optimization's Geometry
authors: Zhou He
abstract: ArXiv:2608.18129v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study simulation-optimization of systems of optimizers (SOSO): agent-based simulations in which every agent solves a structured optimization - a linear program (LP), mixed-integer program, or dynamic program - at every decision epoch. Such systems arise in supply chains, electricity markets, and logistics, yet standard simulation optimization treats the simulation as a black box, discarding the inner optimization's geometry. We formalize SOSO and develop a framework that converts this geometry into computational advantage. We prove that the inner LP's optimal basis and dual variables propagate through the dynamics to yield an exact, unbiased, single-replication infinitesimal perturbation analysis (IPA) gradient of the outer objective, with measure-zero basis changes as the only obstructions. We derive a common-random-numbers covariance bound governed by a computable basis-disagreement count from the forward simulation. We further prove that IPA variance grows exponentially with feedback depth, formalizing the bullwhip effect, and introduce surrogate-as-decision with an error budget unifying LP-horizon and reinforcement-learning surrogates under one bound. We compose these into PRIME, a stochastic-approximation solver integrating the IPA gradient, adaptive step sizing, and multi-start spatial diversification. On six testbeds spanning the SOSO taxonomy, PRIME achieves the best or tied-best optimality gap at equal budget with near-zero oscillation and narrow seed-to-seed variance; IPA yields a ~2000x per-replication variance reduction over independent finite differences, and common random numbers cut paired-difference variance by over 10,000x in a 1,000-SKU, six-distribution-center supply chain. These results establish exploiting embedded-optimization geometry as a practically significant direction for simulation optimization.
tldr: 该论文提出了一种利用内层优化几何结构的仿真优化框架，用于求解由多个优化器组成的系统。
motivation: 标准仿真优化将仿真视为黑盒，丢弃了内层优化的几何结构，限制了效率。
method: 提出了SOSO形式化，证明了基于内层LP最优基和对偶变量的IPA梯度，并引入了PRIME求解器。
result: 在多个测试台上，PRIME实现了最佳或并列最佳的优化差距，方差大幅降低。
conclusion: 利用嵌入优化的几何结构是仿真优化中实用的方向。

title: Inverse Born Series Based Neural Operators
authors: John C Schotland, Aseel Titi, Jenn-Nan Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2608.18262v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The inverse Born series provides a general perturbative framework for representing nonlinear inverse maps between infinite-dimensional function spaces and has found numerous applications in inverse problems governed by partial differential equations and integral equations. Motivated by its operator-theoretic structure, we develop a systematic framework for constructing neural operators that approximate the operator expansions arising in the inverse Born series. Our approach combines the analytical representation of the inverse Born series with the expressive power of neural operators, yielding data-driven approximations of the nonlinear inverse map while preserving the underlying operator structure. The proposed framework is applicable to a broad class of inverse problems and is presented in a general functional-analytic setting. To demonstrate its practical performance, we consider two representative examples: inverse scattering and the Calder\'on (electrical impedance tomography) problem. Numerical experiments show that the constructed neural operators accurately approximate the inverse Born expansions and produce high-quality reconstructions across a range of test cases. These results indicate that the proposed methodology provides an effective and computationally efficient approach for learning nonlinear inverse operators and suggests a promising direction for integrating classical operator expansions with modern neural operator architectures.
tldr: This paper develops a framework for constructing neural operators that approximate the inverse Born series for solving nonlinear inverse problems.
motivation: The inverse Born series provides a general perturbative framework for nonlinear inverse maps, and the authors aim to integrate this with neural operators to leverage both analytical structure and data-driven expressive power.
method: They combine the analytical representation of the inverse Born series with neural operators, presenting a functional-analytic framework, and apply it to inverse scattering and the Calderón problem.
result: Numerical experiments show that the constructed neural operators accurately approximate the inverse Born expansions and produce high-quality reconstructions.
conclusion: The methodology offers an effective and computationally efficient approach for learning nonlinear inverse operators, suggesting a promising direction for integrating classical operator expansions with modern neural operator architectures.

title: Finite-player Optimal Stopping Games: Randomization, $\alpha$-potentiality, And Learning
authors: Xin Guo, Mehdi Talbi, Qinxin Yan
abstract: ArXiv:2608.18355v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Finite-player nonzero-sum optimal stopping games typically lead to coupled equilibrium systems whose complexity grows rapidly with the number of players. We introduce an independently randomized formulation in which each stopping rule is represented by an adapted, nondecreasing cumulative stopping process. The canonical embedding preserves pure-profile payoffs, and a pure profile is a Nash equilibrium of the original game if and only if its embedding is a Nash equilibrium of the randomized game. We adopt the [MATH]-potential approach to construct an [MATH]-potential function, with the error [MATH] under weak-interaction. We also identify an exact-potential subclass with a closed-form threshold equilibrium. For local stopped-status interactions, randomized payoffs admit a local stopped-mass representation, and potential maximization can be formulated as a multidimensional singular-control problem with local gradient constraints and a nonlocal condition for finite jumps. Under suitable regularity assumptions, we study the associated Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman quasi-variational inequality and its regularity properties. For unknown model coefficients, we propose a bounded-intensity Potential-CT-DDPG learning algorithm. Numerical experiments closely match the analytical benchmark and yield estimated best-response improvements consistent with [MATH] scaling.
tldr: This paper introduces an independently randomized formulation for finite-player nonzero-sum optimal stopping games and studies potential-based equilibria and learning algorithms.
motivation: The complexity of coupled equilibrium systems in multi-player optimal stopping games grows rapidly; the authors propose a randomized formulation to simplify analysis and enable learning.
method: They use a canonical embedding of stopping times into cumulative stopping processes, define a potential function for a class of games, and analyze the HJB quasi-variational inequality for local stopped-status interactions. They also propose a bounded-intensity Potential-CT-DDPG learning algorithm.
result: They show that pure-profile equilibria correspond to equilibria of the randomized game, identify an exact-potential subclass with closed-form threshold equilibrium, and their numerical experiments match analytical benchmarks.
conclusion: The randomized formulation and potential approach provide a tractable framework for analyzing and solving multi-player optimal stopping games, with learning algorithms performing well.

title: Direction-Adaptive Plane-Wave Discontinuous Galerkin Methods For The Helmholtz Equation
authors: Shelvean Kapita
abstract: ArXiv:2608.18380v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider plane-wave discontinuous Galerkin (PWDG) approximations of the Helmholtz equation with adaptive local propagation directions. The directions are chosen by minimizing a weighted residual on the mesh skeleton. We study two formulations: in Part A the PWDG system is solved for the coefficients at fixed directions, while in Part B the same residual is minimized jointly over coefficients and directions, with the coefficients eliminated by variable projection. Complex angles unify propagating and evanescent Trefftz waves. The discrete system is normalized in the Trefftz-DG norm, and a local Cauchy-trace Gramian is used to remove numerically dependent directions. On straight edges the residual integrals are exact. For all-Dirichlet problems, the residual equals the squared DG error and provides local adaptive indicators. We prove local quadratic growth of the reduced direction functional near an identifiable zero-residual solution of fixed rank. Numerically, an exact circular DtN test shows that the dominant phase direction of a Hankel wave can be recovered accurately even when a small plane-wave fan gives a larger field error. We also separate the effects of the coefficient basis, trace cutoff, and trace-spectrum arithmetic on the high-[MATH] DtN floor. Finally, for finite sums of plane waves, residual-based ENRICH--MOVE continuation recovers all directions to roundoff for [MATH]. At [MATH] the automatic birth step enters a false basin, whereas a nearby birth again reaches roundoff. The results indicate that direction adaptation is most effective for solutions of low directional complexity.
tldr: This paper proposes adaptive direction selection in plane-wave discontinuous Galerkin methods for the Helmholtz equation, focusing on numerical accuracy and efficiency.
motivation: To improve the accuracy and efficiency of plane-wave DG methods for the Helmholtz equation by adapting local propagation directions to better match the solution.
method: The authors minimize a weighted residual on the mesh skeleton to choose directions, considering two formulations: fixed directions and joint optimization over coefficients and directions with variable projection. They also use a local Cauchy-trace Gramian to handle numerical dependencies.
result: The method accurately recovers dominant phase directions for a Hankel wave, even when a small fan gives larger field errors, and residual-based continuation achieves roundoff accuracy for finite sums of plane waves at certain parameters.
conclusion: Direction adaptation is most effective for solutions with low directional complexity, suggesting its usefulness in reducing computational cost while maintaining accuracy.

title: Boundaries Of Logarithmic Voronoi Cells Can Be Transcendental
authors: Yulia Alexandr
abstract: ArXiv:2608.18434v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that logarithmic Voronoi boundaries for one-dimensional algebraic models in the probability simplex need not be algebraic. We give two explicit examples. For a union of two lines, the logarithmic Voronoi cell at a specific smooth rational point has a transcendental boundary point. For a cuspidal curve, the cell at the singular point contains a non-algebraic real-analytic boundary branch.
tldr: The paper demonstrates that logarithmic Voronoi boundaries for certain algebraic models need not be algebraic, providing explicit counterexamples.
motivation: To address whether logarithmic Voronoi cells of algebraic models in the probability simplex are always algebraic, which is a question in algebraic statistics.
method: The author constructs two explicit examples: a union of two lines and a cuspidal curve, and analyzes the corresponding logarithmic Voronoi cells.
result: For a union of two lines, a transcendental boundary point exists at a smooth rational point; for a cuspidal curve, a non-algebraic real-analytic boundary branch appears.
conclusion: Logarithmic Voronoi boundaries are not necessarily algebraic, contradicting possible expectations and highlighting complexities in algebraic statistics.

title: Data-Driven Output Feedback Based Analysis And Control For Unknown Discrete-Time Linear System
authors: Jie Huang Haoyan Lin
abstract: ArXiv:2608.18452v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Using the notion of data informativity, the existing results have given conditions under which the data are informative for controller designs for various control problems of unknown linear discrete-time systems, and have developed methods to compute such controllers from data. Nevertheless, the existing conditions for computing a dynamic output feedback control law based on the input and output data are somehow stringent. In this paper, we first focus on developing data informativity analysis and control for an unknown system with a known input matrix. It turns out that the informativity conditions for such a system are much milder and the methods for computing state feedback control laws for stabilization, deadbeat control, and the linear-quadratic regulator (LQR) for such a system are much more straightforward. Further, based on the parameterized observer, we show that the problem of computing a dynamic output feedback control law for an unknown system can be converted to the problem of designing a state feedback control law for an ancillary system whose input matrix is known. Therefore, the results of the first part of this paper can be directly used to compute a dynamic output feedback control law for stabilization and deadbeat control for unknown linear discrete-time systems based on the input and output data. Moreover, we present a dynamic output feedback control law which will asymptotically approach a state feedback LQR solution to the original unknown system.
tldr: This paper develops data-driven methods for analysis and control of unknown discrete-time linear systems using input-output data, focusing on state and output feedback designs.
motivation: Existing conditions for computing dynamic output feedback control from data are stringent, and the authors aim to relax these by assuming a known input matrix and using parameterized observers.
method: They develop data informativity analysis for systems with known input matrix, derive simpler conditions for state feedback designs (stabilization, deadbeat, LQR), and convert output feedback design to state feedback for an ancillary system.
result: The proposed approach yields milder informativity conditions and straightforward methods for computing dynamic output feedback control laws, including an output feedback that asymptotically approaches a state feedback LQR solution.
conclusion: The paper provides a practical and less restrictive framework for data-driven control of unknown linear systems, enabling output feedback controller design from data.

title: Isomorphisms Between Symmetric Spaces Over Infinite And Finite Von Neumann Algebras
authors: Jinghao Huang, Fedor Sukochev, Dmitriy Zanin
abstract: ArXiv:2608.18460v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The primary aim of this paper is to show a linear topological isomorphism between (elements of a wide class {of}) symmetric spaces over the hyperfinite [MATH] factor [MATH] and certain symmetric operator space over the hyperfinite [MATH] factor [MATH]. Precisely, we show that for any symmetric function space [MATH] (in the sense of Lindenstrauss and Tzafriri) such that both [MATH] and its K\"othe dual have the Kruglov property, the symmetric operator space [MATH] is isomorphic to some symmetric space [MATH]. This result establishes a noncommutative version of a well-known result due to Johnson, Maurey, Schechtman and Tzafriri, and answers the noncommutative version of a question due to Mityagin.
tldr: This paper establishes a linear topological isomorphism between symmetric function spaces over the hyperfinite II_1 factor and certain symmetric operator spaces, providing a noncommutative analogue of a classical result.
motivation: The authors aim to extend the Johnson-Maurey-Schechtman-Tzafriri theorem to the noncommutative setting and to answer a question posed by Mityagin regarding the structure of symmetric spaces over von Neumann algebras.
method: They consider symmetric function spaces (in the sense of Lindenstrauss and Tzafriri) whose Kothe dual also has the Kruglov property, and construct an isomorphism to symmetric operator spaces over the hyperfinite factor.
result: For any such symmetric function space, the corresponding symmetric operator space is isomorphic to some symmetric space, proving the noncommutative version of the classical result.
conclusion: The work resolves the noncommutative question and establishes a broad class of isomorphisms, contributing to the theory of noncommutative symmetric spaces.

title: A Simple Geometric Proof Of Kepler's First Law
authors: Hyouggyu Choi
abstract: ArXiv:2608.18537v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a simple geometric proof of Kepler's first law. The core of the argument rests on a kinematic invariant that we call the velocity projection ratio - the ratio between the radial projection of the velocity and its projection onto a fixed direction parallel to the periapsis line. We show that the constancy of this ratio is an immediate consequence of Newton's laws, and that it leads directly to the focus-directrix property of the orbit. By establishing a direct link between planetary dynamics and the classical geometric definition of conics, our proof reveals the conic nature of the orbit as an inevitable consequence of the inverse-square law.
tldr: A geometric proof of Kepler's first law using a kinematic invariant called the velocity projection ratio.
motivation: To provide a simple and intuitive geometric proof of Kepler's first law directly from Newton's laws of motion.
method: Introduces the velocity projection ratio, shows its constancy as a consequence of Newton's laws, and derives the focus-directrix property of conic sections.
result: Demonstrates that the orbit under an inverse-square force is a conic section, with bound orbits being ellipses.
conclusion: The proof links planetary dynamics to the classical geometric definition of conics, revealing the conic nature as an inevitable consequence of the inverse-square law.

title: Symmetry Of Solutions And Domain-Reduction Finite Element Method For Second-Order Linear Elliptic Dirichlet Boundary Value Problems On Bounded Domains
authors: Wei Jiang Xianlong Pan
abstract: ArXiv:2608.18549v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Combining classical group theory and partial differential equation theory, this paper investigates the symmetry group [MATH] of the unique solution [MATH] to the second-order linear elliptic boundary value problem on an [MATH]-dimensional bounded domain [MATH] [MATH], [MATH], The following symmetry groups are defined and characterized respectively: the symmetry group [MATH] of the second-order coefficient matrix function [MATH]; the symmetry group [MATH] of the first-order coefficient column vector function [MATH]; the symmetry group [MATH] of the zero-order coefficient function [MATH]; the symmetry group [MATH] of the internal source function [MATH]; and the symmetry group [MATH] of the boundary source function [MATH]. This paper rigorously proves that the common symmetry group [MATH] is a subgroup of [MATH]. In addition, if the common symmetry group contains several mirror symmetry elements, the original second-order linear elliptic boundary value problem on the entire domain [MATH] can be reduced to the corresponding boundary value problem on a certain subdomain. It is strictly proven in this paper that the new boundary condition imposed on the boundary of the subdomain is the homogeneous generalized Neumann boundary condition. The linear finite element method is used to numerically solve the second-order linear elliptic boundary value problem on the subdomain, thereby achieving domain reduction and significantly reducing the computational cost.
tldr: This paper studies symmetry groups of solutions to second-order linear elliptic boundary value problems and proposes a domain-reduction finite element method to reduce computational cost.
motivation: The authors aim to exploit solution symmetries to reduce the computational domain for elliptic boundary value problems, thereby improving numerical efficiency.
method: They define and characterize symmetry groups of coefficient functions and source terms, prove that the common symmetry group is a subgroup of the solution's symmetry group, and derive homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions for the reduced subdomain. Then they apply the linear finite element method to solve the reduced problem.
result: It is rigorously proven that mirror symmetry in the problem allows reduction to a subdomain with homogeneous generalized Neumann boundary conditions, and numerical experiments demonstrate significant computational cost savings.
conclusion: The domain-reduction approach leveraging symmetry is effective for second-order linear elliptic problems, but the work is purely classical/applied mathematics with no connection to quantum information or related research directions.

title: Convergent Series Of Coherent States
authors: Peter Vang Uttenthal
abstract: ArXiv:2608.18559v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For a discrete subspace [MATH] of a homogeneous space [MATH] and a positive definite reproducing kernel Hilbert space [MATH], a convergence proof is given for series of partial Whitney functions over [MATH] that arise in the span of coherent states in [MATH].
tldr: This paper proves convergence of series of partial Whitney functions in coherent state spans over discrete subspaces in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces.
motivation: The paper addresses a mathematical question about convergence in the context of coherent states and reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, likely motivated by theoretical physics but without direct application to the specified research directions.
method: The author provides a convergence proof for series of partial Whitney functions over discrete subspaces in the span of coherent states, using properties of positive definite reproducing kernels.
result: A formal convergence result is established for such series.
conclusion: The work is purely mathematical and does not connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Affine Evaluation Maps, Dimension Groups, And Fair Measures
authors: Eli Glasner
abstract: ArXiv:2608.18700v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be a Cantor space and let [MATH] be a compact Choquet simplex of atomless full-support probability measures. We introduce the associated (AEM), which assigns to each clopen set [MATH] the affine function \[ \widehat A(\mu)=\mu(A),\qquad \mu\in Q, \] and study the geometric subset condition obtained by comparing these evaluation functions pointwise on [MATH]. For a good geometric AEM we construct the ordered group \[ G_Q=C(X,\mathbb Z)/N_Q, \qquad N_Q=\left\{f\in C(X,\mathbb Z): \int f\,d\mu=0\ \mu\in Q\right\}, \] and show that it is a simple dimension group whose normalized state space is canonically [MATH]. We prove that its order interval [MATH] is precisely the clopen scale and that \[ J_Q=N_Q, \] where [MATH] is generated by the elementary relations [MATH] with [MATH]. We also show that the full stabilizer [MATH] has invariant-measure simplex exactly [MATH]. Using the clopen-scale property and the Herman--Putnam--Skau realization theorem, we obtain a dimension-group proof that every good geometric AEM is realized by a minimal Cantor homeomorphism [MATH] with [MATH]. For a Cantor minimal system we identify [MATH] with the classical dimension group modulo infinitesimals. We further distinguish goodness, fairness, ergodicity, and minimality of the measure stabilizer by explicit examples. Finally, we apply the AEM framework to minimal Cantor actions of countable amenable groups. If [MATH], then [MATH] canonically defines a proper geometric AEM, and we clarify which parts of the preceding theory depend only on [MATH] and which are specifically [MATH]-dynamical. In particular, [MATH] is good if and only if there exists a minimal homeomorphism [MATH] of [MATH] such that \[ M_T(X)=M_G(X). \].
tldr: This paper studies affine evaluation maps and dimension groups associated with Cantor spaces and Choquet simplices, focusing on geometric conditions and realizations by minimal Cantor homeomorphisms.
motivation: The research interests are centered on quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, and hybrid quantum systems, none of which relate to topological dynamics or dimension groups.
method: Introduces affine evaluation maps on clopen sets, constructs an ordered group from functions with zero integrals over a simplex of measures, and proves properties of this dimension group.
result: Proves that the constructed group is a simple dimension group whose state space is the simplex, and that good geometric AEMs are realized by minimal Cantor systems, extending to countable amenable group actions.
conclusion: The work contributes to the theory of Cantor minimal systems and dimension groups, with no relevance to the specified research directions.

title: Modeling Network Congestion Under Demand Uncertainty Using Wardrop Principles
authors: Yasmine Beck, Francesca Giancola, Ivana Ljubi\'c, Sara Mattia
abstract: ArXiv:2608.18708v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Motivated by the need for reliable traffic management under fluctuating travel demand, we study the problem of determining the worst-case congestion in a multi-commodity traffic network subject to demand uncertainty. To this end, we stress-test a given network by identifying demand realizations and corresponding travelers' route choices that maximize congestion. The users of the traffic network are assumed to act according to one of the two Wardrop principles, the user equilibrium or the system optimum, so that the resulting congestion models can be seen as bilevel problems with a single leader and multiple followers. To address uncertain travel demand, we consider different models such as ellipsoidal or budgeted uncertainty sets and the hose polyhedron. We present single-level mixed-integer nonlinear reformulations of the congestion models that exploit binary variables and big-M constants, prove the existence of optimal solutions, derive valid big-Ms, and propose several enhancement techniques to further strengthen the formulations. An extensive computational study on instances of the Sioux Falls network and instances from the SNDlib demonstrates the computational effectiveness of the proposed techniques and provides insight into the impact of different congestion measures and uncertainty models on the resulting worst-case congestion.
tldr: This paper develops optimization models to stress-test traffic networks under uncertain demand using bilevel programming with Wardrop principles.
motivation: To address the need for reliable traffic management under fluctuating travel demand and to identify worst-case congestion scenarios.
method: Formulates bilevel congestion models with demand uncertainty sets (ellipsoidal, budgeted, hose), reformulates them as single-level mixed-integer nonlinear programs using binary variables and big-M constants, and proposes enhancement techniques.
result: Presents valid big-Ms and strengthened formulations, demonstrating computational effectiveness on Sioux Falls and SNDlib instances.
conclusion: The proposed techniques efficiently compute worst-case congestion and reveal the impact of different congestion measures and uncertainty models.

title: Joint Power Allocation And Phase-Shift Design For Beyond-Diagonal Stacked Intelligent Metasurfaces-Aided Isac Systems
authors: Yuhui Jiao, Qian Zhang, Xuejun Cheng, Meihui Liu, Jiancheng An, Ju Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2608.18713v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stacked intelligent metasurfaces (SIM) provide an efficient architecture for integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) with few radio-frequency (RF) chains. However, diagonal SIM provide only element-wise phase control, so balancing multiuser communication and sensing performance may require additional layers. In this letter, we propose a beyond-diagonal SIM (BD-SIM) architecture for ISAC, enabling controllable intra-layer coupling through reconfigurable impedance networks, thereby enhancing wave-domain processing flexibility. We develop a unified alternating optimization framework applicable to fully-connected, group-connected, and diagonal SIM architectures. Within this framework, we derive a closed-form power allocation rule and propose an effective variable separation algorithm for multi-layer phase-shift design. Simulation results show that the proposed BD-SIM achieve a better communication-sensing trade-off and require fewer layers to attain performance comparable to conventional SIM.
tldr: The paper proposes a beyond-diagonal stacked intelligent metasurface (BD-SIM) architecture for integrated sensing and communication (ISAC), along with a joint power allocation and phase-shift optimization framework that outperforms conventional diagonal SIM in communication-sensing trade-offs.
motivation: Conventional diagonal SIM only provides element-wise phase control, which may require additional layers to balance multiuser communication and sensing. The goal is to enhance wave-domain processing flexibility and improve the trade-off.
method: The authors propose a BD-SIM architecture with reconfigurable impedance networks for controllable intra-layer coupling, and develop a unified alternating optimization framework covering fully-connected, group-connected, and diagonal SIM architectures. They derive a closed-form power allocation rule and a variable separation algorithm for multi-layer phase-shift design.
result: Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed BD-SIM achieves a better communication-sensing trade-off and requires fewer layers to attain performance comparable to conventional SIM.
conclusion: The BD-SIM architecture offers enhanced flexibility and efficiency for ISAC systems, but the work is outside the specified quantum information and thermodynamics research areas.

title: Maximal Attractors For Perturbations Of Unimodal Maps Near A Homoclinic Tangency
authors: Przemys{\l}aw Kucharski
abstract: ArXiv:2608.18761v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that small planar perturbations of families of unimodal maps have maximal (equal to the intersection of the iterates of their trapping region) attractors at parameters near homoclinic tangency of one of the fixed points. The results hold for general unimodal maps exhibiting certain hyperbolic properties. Hence, admissible families considered include H\'enon-like families, Lozi-like families, or perturbations of border collision normal forms. Therefore, our results generalize results of Viana in the case of H\'enon-like families and Glendinning and Simpson in the case of border collision normal forms.
tldr: This paper proves the existence of maximal attractors in small planar perturbations of unimodal maps near homoclinic tangency, generalizing previous results to broader families.
motivation: To understand the dynamics of perturbed unimodal maps and characterize attractors near homoclinic tangency, extending results from specific families like Hénon-like maps.
method: The authors analyze perturbations of general unimodal maps satisfying certain hyperbolic properties, using techniques from dynamical systems to establish the existence of maximal attractors.
result: They show that for a wide class of families (including Hénon-like, Lozi-like, and border collision normal forms), there exist maximal attractors at parameters near homoclinic tangency.
conclusion: The results generalize earlier findings, providing a unified framework for understanding attractor behavior in perturbed unimodal maps.

title: Model Card For OpenAI Privacy Filter
authors: Charles de Bourcy, Sahra Ghalebikesabi, Avi Schwarzschild, Alex Gorbachev, Mihai Maruseac, Annie Chu, Vol Kyrylov, Tong Mu, Ally Bennett, Andy Nguyen, Casey Meehan, Jessica Gan Lee, Shane Bauer, Harold Nguyen, Rodolpho Eckhardt, Yuqi Liu, Charlie Oxborough, Marco Rougeth, Omar Chedid, Caio Costa, Yash Parikh, Yao Li, Congzheng Song, Om Thakkar, Vinnie Monaco
abstract: ArXiv:2608.18274v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: OpenAI Privacy Filter is a compact, bidirectional token-classification model for detecting and redacting personally identifiable information (PII) and secrets in unstructured text. The model is derived from an autoregressively pretrained checkpoint and converted into a bidirectional, banded-attention classifier that labels an input sequence in a single forward pass. A constrained Viterbi decoder produces coherent spans across eight privacy categories and exposes configurable operating points for precision-recall tradeoffs. Privacy Filter has 1.5 billion total parameters, 50 million active parameters per token, and a 128,000-token context window. It is designed for efficient local deployment and domain-specific fine-tuning. Privacy Filter is intended as a configurable data-minimization component within layered privacy workflows, not as an anonymization or compliance guarantee.
tldr: OpenAI Privacy Filter is a compact bidirectional token-classification model for detecting and redacting PII and secrets, with a banded-attention architecture and constrained Viterbi decoding.
motivation: To provide an efficient, configurable data-minimization tool for layered privacy workflows.
method: Derived from an autoregressive pretrained checkpoint, converted to a bidirectional banded-attention classifier, with a constrained Viterbi decoder for coherent spans across eight privacy categories.
result: The model has 1.5B total parameters, 50M active per token, and a 128k-token context window, designed for local deployment and fine-tuning.
conclusion: It is intended as a configurable component in privacy workflows, not as a guarantee of anonymization or compliance.

title: AoNT Trap: Borromean-Entangled Mutable Chameleon Trapdoor Hash All-or-Nothing Stream Cipher
authors: Victor Kebande
abstract: ArXiv:2608.18403v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work introduces the Borromean-Entangled Chameleon Trapdoor Hash All-or-Nothing (AoNT) Stream Cipher (BEC-Trap), a novel construction that merges Borromean interdependence, trapdoor-enabled mutability, and streaming encryption into a unified framework. The (BEC-Trap) cipher links key (K), initialization vector (V ), and internal state (St) in a Borromean structure, ensuring that breaking, guessing, or removing any one component collapses the entire keystream, providing a computational (AoNT) interdependence under standard cryptographic assumptions. A chameleon trapdoor hash is integrated to permit controlled collisions, enabling seamless rekeying, (V ) refresh, and state rotation without resynchronizing endpoints. This design provides confidentiality, forward secrecy, and adaptive key management with low computational overhead, making it suitable for high-throughput secure messaging, IoT communications, and privacy-preserving blockchain channels. Security analysis of the (BEC-Trap) shows that the construction is resistant to key-recovery attacks, state compromise, and desynchronization attempts, delivering a robust cryptographic primitive for next-generation secure communications.
tldr: A classical stream cipher using Borromean entanglement and a chameleon trapdoor hash for mutable encryption.
motivation: To provide a robust cryptographic primitive with forward secrecy and adaptive key management for next-generation secure communications.
method: Combines Borromean interdependence of key, IV, and internal state with a chameleon trapdoor hash to enable controlled collisions and seamless rekeying.
result: Claims resistance to key-recovery, state compromise, and desynchronization, with low computational overhead.
conclusion: Proposes a novel classical cipher, but it is unrelated to the user's research directions in quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Formal Verification Of Romanov's Triplet Logic: A Verified Filter For Sliding-window 3-cnf With Application To Structured Formulas
authors: Dmitry V. Alexandrov
abstract: ArXiv:2608.18445v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present the first mechanised formalisation of Romanov's Triplet Logic (TLS) in the Rocq proof assistant. TLS is a triplet-based combinatorial framework for reasoning about compatible paths through layered triplet structures, called Compact Triplets Structures (CTS), and their intersection via Romanov's Effective Procedure, which we refer to as Simple Vertex Intersection (SVI). Originally motivated by Boolean satisfiability, TLS constitutes a self-contained mathematical theory whose formal properties had not been previously established. We formalise the core of TLS in Rocq, including Compact Triplets Formulas (CTF), CTS, hyperstructures, clearing, and SVI. For the well-formed sliding-window fragment we verify a clause-by-clause CNF-to-CTF translation, the clearing procedure, and aligned intersection, and we prove explicit polynomial-time bounds for the filter stages. Our main contribution is a precise correctness boundary: the existence of a joint satisfying set implies non-emptiness of SVI, but the converse does not hold in general; for aligned structures we recover a complete bi-implication, extended to systems of structures. We also formalise soundness of grouped-window translation and exhibit a formal counterexample to its completeness. We introduce VFR, an extracted OCaml prototype that provides a verified decision procedure for the sliding-window fragment and a sound one-sided filter for general 3-CNF, with a Python runtime and reproducible Docker packaging. Benchmarks on random and structured instances confirm the predicted behaviour, and the complete toolchain is available as a curated Zenodo artifact. The Rocq development comprises more than 23,000 lines of code across seventeen files, with 427 proved lemmas and theorems and zero admitted goals.
tldr: The paper presents a mechanised formalisation of Romanov's Triplet Logic in the Rocq proof assistant, including a verified filter for sliding-window 3-CNF and a prototype decision procedure.
motivation: To provide formal guarantees for Romanov's Triplet Logic, a combinatorial framework for reasoning about compatible paths through layered triplet structures, originally motivated by Boolean satisfiability.
method: Formalise the core of TLS in Rocq, including CTF, CTS, hyperstructures, clearing, and SVI, and verify clause-by-clause CNF-to-CTF translation, clearing procedure, and aligned intersection for the sliding-window fragment, proving polynomial-time bounds.
result: Prove a correctness boundary: existence of a joint satisfying set implies non-emptiness of SVI, but converse not in general; for aligned structures, a complete bi-implication is recovered. Also formalise soundness of grouped-window translation and exhibit a counterexample to its completeness.
conclusion: Provide a verified decision procedure for the sliding-window fragment and a sound one-sided filter for general 3-CNF, with an extracted OCaml prototype and reproducible packaging.

title: Hardness Of Forcing Unique Perfect Matchings In Bipartite Graphs Of Maximum Degree 3
authors: Ryoma Aoshima, Takashi Horiyama, Atsuki Nagao, Fumiya Sakamoto, Hibiki Sato, Kazuhisa Seto, Karin Umebayashi
abstract: ArXiv:2608.18617v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In a graph [MATH], a set of edges [MATH] is called a if there exists a unique perfect matching [MATH] such that [MATH]. Similarly, a set of edges [MATH] is called an if the graph with edge set [MATH] has a unique perfect matching. It is known that, given a bipartite graph [MATH] of maximum degree~[MATH] and a perfect matching [MATH], the problem of deciding whether there exists a forcing set of size at most [MATH] for [MATH] is NP-complete. Moreover, given a bipartite graph [MATH] of maximum degree~[MATH] and a perfect matching [MATH], the problem of deciding whether there exists an anti-forcing set of size at most [MATH] for [MATH] is NP-complete. Furthermore, given a bipartite graph of maximum degree~[MATH], the problem of deciding whether there exists a perfect matching [MATH] that can be made unique by a forcing set of size at most [MATH] is also NP-complete. In contrast, the computational complexity of deciding whether there exists a perfect matching [MATH] that can be made unique by an anti-forcing set of size at most [MATH] is not known, even for general graphs. In this paper, we show that all of these problems remain NP-complete even when restricted to bipartite graphs of maximum degree~[MATH].
tldr: This paper proves NP-completeness for problems involving forcing and anti-forcing sets that ensure a unique perfect matching in bipartite graphs of maximum degree 3.
motivation: To determine the computational complexity of deciding whether a given perfect matching can be made unique by small forcing or anti-forcing sets, which has applications in chemistry and combinatorial optimization.
method: The authors employ polynomial-time reductions from known NP-complete problems, constructing instances that are bipartite with maximum degree 3.
result: All the decision problems considered remain NP-complete even when restricted to bipartite graphs of maximum degree 3.
conclusion: The hardness results are strengthened to a restricted graph class, resolving open questions about the complexity of these problems in a more constrained setting.

title: IriSig-Spoof: A Real-World Benchmark For Time-Robust Satellite Rf Fingerprinting And Spoofing Detection
authors: Shichang Guo, Yuanyu Zhang, Shuangrui Zhao, Ji He, Pinchang Zhang, Yulong Shen
abstract: ArXiv:2608.18642v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite Internet is becoming critical communications infrastructure, yet its open wireless links remain vulnerable to satellite impersonation and signal spoofing. Radio frequency fingerprinting (RFF) offers a potential defense by exploiting transmitter-specific hardware imperfections manifested in received signals. However, the reliability of existing satellite RFF methods remains difficult to assess because no unified dataset and benchmark support temporal, open-set, and cross-scenario evaluation. To address this gap, we introduce IriSig-Spoof, a real-world Iridium dataset comprising 5.17 million messages collected from 66 satellites over 32 days, together with software-defined radio (SDR)-generated spoofing signals from indoor and outdoor settings. We further establish three benchmark tasks: temporal robustness evaluation, open-set RFF identification with unknown-signal rejection, and cross-scenario spoofing detection. Experiments using a multi-scale attention convolutional neural network (MACNN) show that temporal robustness varies across configurations, with the best configuration achieving 97.75% average cross-day accuracy. In open-set evaluation, MACNN achieves an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.9715, while showing that effective unknown-signal rejection does not necessarily ensure reliable identity assignment. Cross-scenario experiments reveal differences at low false-positive rates. IriSig-Spoof provides a reproducible basis for evaluating robust RFF methods under temporal variation and changing attack conditions.
tldr: Introduces IriSig-Spoof, a real-world benchmark for evaluating satellite RF fingerprinting and spoofing detection methods using Iridium satellite data.
motivation: The reliability of existing satellite RFF methods is difficult to assess due to lack of unified datasets and benchmarks supporting temporal, open-set, and cross-scenario evaluation.
method: Collects 5.17 million messages from 66 Iridium satellites over 32 days, generates SDR-based spoofing signals, and establishes three benchmark tasks; uses a multi-scale attention convolutional neural network (MACNN) for evaluation.
result: Best configuration achieves 97.75% cross-day accuracy, open-set AUROC of 0.9715, and reveals differences in cross-scenario detection at low false-positive rates.
conclusion: IriSig-Spoof provides a reproducible basis for evaluating robust RFF methods under temporal variation and changing attack conditions.

title: Improving LLM-Based Ssh Honeypots Through Prompting And Fine-Tuning
authors: Muris Sladi\'c, Veronica Valeros, Eman Alibali\'c, Sebastian Garcia
abstract: ArXiv:2608.18686v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-based SSH honeypots often use closed cloud LLMs because they give strong shell realism, but cloud models create deployment problems. These include no stable versioning, provider-side changes, attacker-driven cost, and model decommissioning. Local open-weight models avoid these problems, but they usually perform worse and make mistakes that reveal the honeypot. These mistakes include malformed outputs, command echoing, inconsistent filesystem state, and AI-style artifacts. This paper studies how to improve and evaluate the shell emulation accuracy of local LLM-based SSH honeypots using prompt design and supervised fine-tuning. We fine-tune and evaluate eight models in total: the original fine-tuned GPT-3.5 model used in shelLM and seven open-weight local models, each compared to its base model. We also test how prompt structure transfers across model families. Using 34 automated unit tests that measure shell emulation accuracy in single-session and fresh-session settings, we find that prompt design has a large effect and that fine-tuning depends on dataset coverage. Fine-tuning on the original 112-conversation dataset does not improve aggregate pass rate, while an expanded dataset built from honeypot logs produces clearly stronger local models. Taken together, the results suggest that prompting and fine-tuning can each improve local LLM honeypots on their own, but their effects do not combine straightforwardly, since strong rule-based prompting and supervised adaptation can also conflict by addressing overlapping shell-behavior constraints.
tldr: This paper studies how to improve local LLM-based SSH honeypots using prompt design and supervised fine-tuning, finding that both can help but their effects do not combine straightforwardly.
motivation: Closed cloud LLMs used in SSH honeypots have deployment issues, while local open-weight models are less accurate and reveal the honeypot. The goal is to improve shell emulation accuracy of local models.
method: The authors fine-tune and evaluate eight models, including a fine-tuned GPT-3.5 and seven open-weight local models. They use 34 automated unit tests to measure shell emulation accuracy in single-session and fresh-session settings, and test prompt design and dataset coverage.
result: Prompt design has a large effect, and fine-tuning with an expanded dataset from honeypot logs produces stronger local models, but fine-tuning on the original dataset does not improve aggregate pass rate. Effects of prompting and fine-tuning do not combine straightforwardly.
conclusion: Local LLM honeypots can be improved by both prompting and fine-tuning, but their interaction requires careful consideration since they may address overlapping shell-behavior constraints.

title: Catastrophic Learning: A New Attack Vector On Continual Learning Networks
authors: Niklas Bunzel Benedikt Kluss
abstract: ArXiv:2608.18976v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continual Learning (CL) enables deep learning models to iteratively learn from a stream of data without forgetting prior knowledge. Existing adversarial research on CL primarily aims to re-enable catastrophic forgetting, attacking stability and reducing availability. We identify a novel security flaw: data manipulated by an attacker can reduce the learnability of current or upcoming iterations. We term such manipulations learning blockers, as they attack the plasticity of CL algorithms. They are particularly harmful because they are difficult to detect during training of the current iteration, since they can target iterations whose data the model has not yet encountered. When learning blockers additionally induce catastrophic forgetting, the resulting overall degradation is what we call catastrophic learning. We formalize this scenario, define a threat model and propose six attack strategies: Label-Exchange, Tensor-Exchange, Attraction-Coincident, Attraction-Preceding, Repulsion-Coincident, and Repulsion-Preceding. The Attraction variants minimize the loss between the poisoned and the victim iteration label, pulling their representations together in feature space; the Repulsion variants maximize this loss, pushing them apart so stability mechanisms resist the required parameter shift. In the Coincident variants, the poisoned and the victim iteration coincide, using a clean reference iteration only as a label source; in the Preceding variants, the poisoned iteration precedes the victim, leaving it unlearnable due to distorted representations. We evaluate on MNIST and Split-CIFAR10 against three CL strategies - DER, ER-ACE, and iCaRL - across more than 4,480 simulations. Our results demonstrate a strong vulnerability: an adversary can selectively impede plasticity to hinder the acquisition of new knowledge, while promoting loss of prior knowledge, inducing a catastrophic learning scenario.
tldr: This paper introduces a novel class of adversarial attacks on continual learning models, termed 'learning blockers', which manipulate training data to reduce learnability and induce catastrophic forgetting, resulting in 'catastrophic learning'.
motivation: Existing adversarial research on continual learning primarily focuses on causing catastrophic forgetting, but this paper identifies a gap: attacks that target the plasticity of CL algorithms to hinder learning of future iterations, a security flaw not previously addressed.
method: The authors formalize a threat model and propose six attack strategies (Label-Exchange, Tensor-Exchange, Attraction-Coincident, Attraction-Preceding, Repulsion-Coincident, and Repulsion-Preceding) that manipulate training data to either pull representations together or push them apart, evaluated on MNIST and Split-CIFAR10 against three CL strategies (DER, ER-ACE, iCaRL) over 4,480 simulations.
result: The results demonstrate a strong vulnerability: an adversary can selectively impede plasticity to hinder new knowledge acquisition while promoting loss of prior knowledge, inducing catastrophic learning.
conclusion: The paper highlights a new security flaw in continual learning and proposes concrete attack strategies, suggesting the need for robust CL algorithms against such manipulations.

title: From Threat Intelligence To Detection: Knowledge-driven Enrichment And Template-based Rule Grounding For Automated Sigma Rule Generation
authors: Sepehr Ghaffarzadegan, Boubakr Nour, Makan Pourzandi, Mourad Debbabi, Chadi Assi
abstract: ArXiv:2608.19011v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mechanisms for dynamically converting cyber threat intelligence (CTI) into actionable detection capabilities are necessary due to the rapid evolution of Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs). Sigma rules are an essential part of contemporary threat detection workflows because they offer a platform-independent framework for expressing detection logic that can be converted into particular queries across SIEM systems. Conventional techniques for manually crafting Sigma rules are prone to mistakes, and necessitate extensive knowledge, which restricts their scalability. Although there are open-source and industry-maintained Sigma rule repositories, they often fail to keep pace with emerging threats and require frequent customization to fit diverse operational environments. This emphasizes the necessity of dynamic rule generation that is adapted to evolving attack techniques as well as particular use cases. In this work, we design AUTOSIGMA, an automated solution for transforming unstructured CTI reports into relevant Sigma rules. Rather than relying solely on language models, AUTOSIGMA leverages a structured knowledge base to enrich partial inputs, matches the enriched content against a repository of existing Sigma rules, and then employs an LLM-as-a-Judge mechanism to iteratively validate the rules. By combining knowledge-driven enrichment, template-based rule grounding, and a multi-stage solution, AUTOSIGMA enables accurate, context-aware, and relevant rule generation. Evaluations across multiple real-world APT reports and multiple security blogs demonstrate that AUTOSIGMA outperforms alternative solutions and LLM models in rule validity, rule relevancy, MITRE ATT&CK technique coverage, and robustness to input quality. AUTOSIGMA's Demo: [URL].
tldr: Presents AUTOSIGMA, an automated system that converts unstructured cyber threat intelligence reports into Sigma rules using knowledge enrichment and LLM validation.
motivation: Rapid evolution of APTs requires dynamic generation of detection rules, but manual crafting is error-prone and not scalable.
method: Combines a structured knowledge base to enrich partial inputs, matches enhanced content against existing Sigma rules, and uses LLM-as-a-Judge for iterative validation.
result: Outperforms alternative solutions in rule validity, relevance, MITRE ATT&CK coverage, and robustness.
conclusion: Provides accurate, context-aware Sigma rule generation to keep pace with emerging threats.

title: FedGuard-DC: Privacy-Preserving Federated Load Forecasting And Cyber-Attack Detection For Data-Center Loads In Transmission Systems
authors: Md Rubel Ahmed Md Kibria Saroare
abstract: ArXiv:2608.19155v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid growth of large data-center (DC) loads is creating new challenges for power-system visibility, privacy, and cyber-physical security. System operators need accurate short-term information about these fast-varying loads, while DC operators may avoid sharing raw megawatt measurements because they can reveal sensitive workload and utilization patterns. This paper presents FedGuard-DC, a federated learning (FL) framework for privacy-preserving DC load forecasting and local false-data-injection attack (FDIA) detection. Each DC trains a dual-head model on its own measurements, where a shared encoder supports both a forecasting head and a reconstruction head. A calibrated anomaly score combines forecast residual and reconstruction error to detect corrupted measurements locally. Raw measurements and absolute MW demand remain at each DC, while only model updates are shared with the global controller. Optional differential privacy and robust trimmed-mean aggregation are included to evaluate privacy-utility behavior and poisoned-client resilience. The framework is validated using EMT simulation data from four large DC loads rated between 150 and 350 MW integrated into the IEEE 39-bus New England system. Results show a 0.5 s-ahead normalized forecast RMSE of 0.023-0.038 pu, compared with 0.32-0.34 pu for persistence. FedGuard-DC detects FDIA with ROC-AUC of 0.979, F1 = 0.930, and precision of 0.988, while robust aggregation reduces the poisoned-client RMSE impact from 0.042 to 0.035 pu.
tldr: FedGuard-DC is a federated learning framework for privacy-preserving load forecasting and false-data-injection detection in data-center loads for power transmission systems.
motivation: Data-center loads are growing and pose challenges for power-system visibility, privacy, and security, as sharing raw measurements can reveal sensitive workload patterns.
method: Each data center trains a dual-head model with a shared encoder for forecasting and reconstruction, using a calibrated anomaly score combining residual and reconstruction error for local FDIA detection, with optional differential privacy and trimmed-mean aggregation to enhance privacy and robustness.
result: Validation on IEEE 39-bus system with four data centers shows low forecast RMSE (0.023-0.038 pu vs 0.32-0.34 for persistence) and high detection performance (ROC-AUC 0.979, F1 0.930, precision 0.988), with robust aggregation mitigating poisoned-client impact.
conclusion: The framework demonstrates effective privacy-preserving forecasting and cyber-attack detection for data-center loads, relevant to power-system security but outside quantum information research interests.

title: Abliteration Mitigation Via Refusal Aliases
authors: Nathan Truong
abstract: ArXiv:2608.18093v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Abliteration, the removal of refusal capabilities from large language models by projecting weight matrices orthogonal to an extracted refusal direction, has emerged as a prominent safety concern through its ability to bypass post-training alignment using only a small set of contrastive prompts. We find that existing defenses commonly overlook the cause of abliteration; that is, how easily the refusal direction can be extracted. To hinder this process, we introduce a weight-editing method that obscures the refusal signal by applying rank-[MATH] updates to residual stream writer matrices while replacing refusal-inducing activations with random aliases and correcting downstream reader matrices to preserve the model's original behavior. On Llama-3-8B, AMRA improves post-abliteration refusal scores by [MATH] points over the undefended baseline with less than [MATH] percentage points of MMLU degradation. On Gemma-2-9B, it improves the post-abliteration refusal by [MATH] points over the baseline while keeping harmful output rates similar to the baseline, albeit at a greater utility cost.
tldr: This paper proposes a weight-editing defense called AMRA to mitigate abliteration in large language models by obscuring the refusal direction and preserving model behavior.
motivation: Existing defenses overlook how easily the refusal direction can be extracted, which is the root cause of abliteration. The goal is to hinder this extraction to prevent bypassing post-training alignment.
method: AMRA applies rank-limited updates to residual stream writer matrices, replaces refusal-inducing activations with random aliases, and corrects downstream reader matrices to preserve original behavior.
result: On Llama-3-8B, AMRA improves post-abliteration refusal scores by a significant margin over the undefended baseline with minimal MMLU degradation; on Gemma-2-9B, it improves refusal scores while keeping harmful output rates similar, albeit at greater utility cost.
conclusion: AMRA is an effective defense against abliteration, though it incurs utility tradeoffs, especially on larger models.

title: Entropy-Constrained Adaptive Stochastic Quantization
authors: Ran Ben Basat, Yaniv Ben-Itzhak, Michael Mitzenmacher, Shay Vargaftik
abstract: ArXiv:2608.18147v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Adaptive stochastic quantization (ASQ) is a recently introduced quantization approach that optimizes the Mean Squared Error (MSE) for a given input while preserving unbiasedness. It is designed to alleviate the communication and memory bottlenecks of modern data and machine learning workloads, including model, gradient, and KV-cache compression and nearest-neighbor search. Further, practical systems can then compress quantized data with a lossless entropy encoder. However, existing unbiased methods, including ASQ, choose their quantization values without considering this later encoding stage, leaving accuracy on the table. We formulate the Entropy Constrained Adaptive Stochastic Quantization (ECASQ) problem, which jointly selects adaptive quantization values to minimize MSE under an entropy budget and an unbiasedness constraint. We give an optimal dynamic program with [MATH] time and [MATH] space for a length-d vector and at most s quantization values, and a GPU-friendly approximate dynamic program with [MATH] time and [MATH] space. The approximation guarantees that the solution has an MSE no larger than the optimal solution that uses one fewer bit of entropy per entry.
